questions.question: How do I classify an AI product's level?
questions.answer: Use the four-step product level assessment in Chapter 6: gather documentation and a demonstration, test what the product does for students rather than what the brochure says, identify the highest defining capability it delivers, and record what student data it needs at that level. The checklist asks, in order: 1. Does it do anything but show fixed content? If not, Level 1. 2. Does it respond to the learner's actions on the page? At least Level 2. 3. Does it keep a record of each student and change what it shows from that record? At least Level 3. 4. Can a student hold an open conversation with it about the material? At least Level 4. 5. Does it generate the content itself, for each student, in real time? Level 5. For example, a product sold as "AI-powered personalized learning" that turns out to be quizzes with feedback and no stored records is Level 2. A vendor's own level claim is a self-report to test, not reject.

questions.question: How should a school start with intelligent textbooks?
questions.answer: Start at Level 2. Interactive textbooks with MicroSims, self-check quizzes, and learning graphs deliver much of the benefit, cost very little, need no student records, and can run offline. Adopting open Level 2 content is one of the book's no-regret moves: it pays off whether or not the AI forecast holds. Move to Level 3 only when the school is ready to govern student data. Chapter 10 gives a governance-readiness check: data minimization, informed consent, a retention policy, clear data ownership, vendor contracts, and a plan for breaches. Add Level 4 chatbot tutoring selectively, where it adds real value, with hint-first guardrails. For example, a middle school might begin with an open Level 2 math textbook in one grade, add a Learning Record Store the following year after the board adopts a retention policy, and pilot a guided chat tutor for one unit after that.

questions.question: How do I design a good pro-social afternoon activity?
questions.answer: Check it against two tests from Chapter 14. The four-feature test asks whether the activity needs other people, has a shared goal, has a real audience or stakes, and ends with reflection. The SAFE check asks whether it is sequenced, active, focused on a personal or social skill, and explicit about its goals. For example, a ten-week ensemble passes both. Students depend on each other, share the goal of a concert, perform for families, and debrief after each rehearsal; the rehearsals build in sequence and name the listening skills being practiced. An open gym where students choose what to do with no adult goals fails both and is the drift the book warns about. Start small: the chapter's ten-week launch plan begins with three activities chosen from student and family surveys, trains adults in SAFE practices and a three-minute debrief, and pilots one block a week before expanding.

questions.question: What makes project-based learning work?
questions.answer: Chapter 14 describes seven essential elements of project-based learning and singles out two as the most important: a driving question and a public exhibition. A driving question is open, important to students, and cannot be answered by a quick search: "How can we cut the food our cafeteria throws away by half?" rather than "What is food waste?" A public exhibition gives the work a real audience and real stakes. High Tech High in San Diego is the book's model: students work in teams on real projects and present them at public exhibitions. Finland's phenomenon-based learning applies a similar idea across subjects, with students studying a real-world topic such as climate or migration through science, math, and language together. Projects also need structure inside the team: shared goals, rotating roles, and individual accountability, so the work does not fall on one student. Chapter 13 gives worked examples of each.

questions.question: How should a school plan and run a pilot?
questions.answer: Write the rules before the pilot starts. Chapter 20 and Chapter 21 recommend: - A school readiness assessment before the pilot begins. - Written pilot goals and a balanced set of success measures, chosen in advance, covering academics, engagement, well-being, equity, and cost. - Pilot governance that names who decides and what would stop the pilot. - A decision rule that says what results mean expand, revise, or end. - A comparison group, ideally through delayed access, and independent evaluation where possible. The pilot risk checklist in Chapter 22 adds one line per known risk, such as screen time, offloading, wrong answers, privacy, equity, job fears, and afternoon drift, with a response for each. For example, a pilot plan with strong academic measures but no measure of afternoon quality has a gap the checklist will catch.

questions.question: What should be in an AI vendor contract?
questions.answer: Chapter 21 lists the clauses that protect students under contract due diligence: how student data may be used (never for advertising, and never shared with unnamed third parties), breach notification within a set time, deletion at the end of the contract, data portability in a standard format, price and price increases, contract term, and what happens when the vendor changes the underlying AI model. The chapter's rule is that two red flags end the conversation. A vendor that claims ownership of student data, refuses deletion, or will not say where data is stored is not one to negotiate with. To avoid vendor lock-in, require open standards and data export, keep terms short, and keep an open Level 2 fallback so the school can leave if it must. The Los Angeles "Ed" chatbot case shows what can happen without these checks.

questions.question: How should a school communicate with families about the change?
questions.answer: Communicate before rumors spread. Chapter 19 recommends a communication calendar that starts before any decision is announced, with family nights, plain-language handouts, and chances to try the tools. Families who first hear about a change through social media fill the gap with their own worst guesses. Be specific and honest. Say what students will do in the morning and the afternoon, how much screen time is involved, what data is collected, where it is stored, and who can see it. Say in advance what the implementation dip may look like. Invite questions you cannot yet answer. inBloom's closure is the cautionary example: it failed because families were not part of the decision. Chapter 10 puts the principle simply: build trust by collecting little, saying what you hold, and acting consistently.

questions.question: How should assessment change in an AI-native school?
questions.answer: Redesign assessment rather than police it. Chapter 20 recommends combining three kinds: - Mastery-based assessment from the morning, where the Learning Record Store shows which concepts each student has mastered. - Performance assessment, where students show a skill by doing it, such as presenting, debating, or building. - Portfolio assessment, a collection of work over time showing growth. Each needs checks for reliability. Chapter 21 gives a teamwork rubric scored by two raters, so afternoon work can be assessed fairly. This approach also answers the cheating problem better than detectors, because a student explaining a design to a panel or revising a draft in class is showing their own thinking. A student's record then shows both what they mastered in the morning and what they built and contributed in the afternoon.

questions.question: How should a district choose a change model?
questions.answer: Match the model to the question. Chapter 16 treats the models as tools for different jobs, not rivals: - Kotter for an ordered leadership plan. - Lewin for the three broad phases and force field analysis. - ADKAR to diagnose one person's missing element. - Bridges for the feelings of loss. - Schein to read the culture. - Senge to build a learning organization. - Fullan for the specifics of schools, including the implementation dip and coherence. - CBAM to track each teacher's concerns and use. Chapter 18 adds that the choice depends on size, culture, history, and time. A small school with high trust might need only Lewin's phases and CBAM. A large district with a history of failed initiatives and change fatigue needs Fullan's coherence framework, fewer connected priorities, and serious capacity building.

questions.question: What can we learn from Estonia's AI Leap?
questions.answer: Estonia's AI Leap (TI-Hüpe), launched in 2025, is a national program giving secondary students and teachers access to AI learning tools along with teacher training. It builds on the country's earlier success bringing computers into schools. The book uses it as the example of a whole system adopting AI on purpose: with a plan, training, and public support. The lesson for districts is coherence. Estonia paired access with training, and built on prior trust and capacity rather than starting cold. Chapter 18 contrasts it with a rapid national mandate in South Korea that, as reported, met resistance. A district can apply the same lessons at its own scale: connect the AI initiative to existing priorities rather than adding it on top, train teachers before students arrive, and build public understanding before rollout. See also Chapter 15.

questions.question: How do I write a school board recommendation for an AI-native pilot?
questions.answer: Chapter 23 gives a one-page outline. A strong recommendation states: 1. The ask: exactly what the board is asked to approve, such as a one-year pilot in two grade-6 classes. 2. The case: the problem the pilot addresses. 3. The evidence, with its level: what is known from randomized trials, what is self-reported, and what is unknown. 4. The risks and responses: one line per risk, from the pilot risk checklist. 5. The equity analysis: who could be helped or left out, and how gaps will be measured. 6. The cost: including devices, staffing, and training, not just software. 7. The decision rule: what results will lead to expansion, revision, or ending. A recommendation that names both sides is more persuasive to a careful board than one that only promises gains. Stating the decision rule in advance also protects the board from being asked to judge the pilot by mood rather than evidence.

questions.question: How do bright spots help lead change?
questions.answer: A bright spot is a person or group already succeeding at something within the system, despite the same constraints as everyone else. Positive deviance is the practice of finding those exceptions and spreading what they do. Both come from the Switch framework in Chapter 19, which describes change as directing the rider (the rational mind), motivating the elephant (emotion), and shaping the path (the environment). Bright spots work because they are proof from inside. For example, if one fifth-grade teacher's students already make strong gains with self-paced practice, other teachers can watch that class, learn the specific moves the teacher makes, and see that it works with students like theirs. That is more persuasive than a vendor's case study from another state. It also respects teachers' expertise, since the solution comes from a colleague rather than from outside.

questions.question: How should formative assessment, spaced practice, and retrieval practice fit an adaptive morning?
questions.answer: These three practices from Chapter 1 are what turn a morning of screen time into lasting learning, so an adaptive textbook should build them in. - Formative assessment uses evidence during learning to change what happens next. In an adaptive textbook, every self-check question is formative: a wrong answer triggers a hint, a different explanation, or a prerequisite review. - Spaced practice spreads review over days and weeks instead of cramming it into one session. - Retrieval practice asks students to recall what they learned, rather than reread it, which strengthens memory. For example, after a student masters a concept on Monday, a well-designed textbook brings back two or three short recall questions on it the following Monday and again a month later, mixed in with new work. If the student misses them, the concept is marked for review rather than left as "mastered." When choosing a product, ask whether its mastery rule ever looks back, or whether a concept passed once stays passed forever. Teachers can apply the same idea in the afternoon by having teams explain earlier concepts from memory as part of a project.

questions.question: How do I build social-emotional learning into afternoon projects?
questions.answer: Social-emotional learning (SEL) covers self-awareness, empathy, perspective taking, relationship skills, and belonging. Chapter 13 finds that these skills are best taught inside real projects rather than in separate lessons, because a real project creates real moments that need them: a disagreement, a teammate who falls behind, an audience to understand. Build them in with structure. Assign team roles that rotate, so every student practices leading, recording, and checking. Teach communication skills such as active listening: paraphrase what a teammate said, ask a clarifying question, and reflect the feeling. Teach conflict resolution by looking at interests rather than positions. End each session with a short reflection naming one thing that went well and one to change. For example, a team building a community garden might hold a mid-project check-in where each member says what they need from the others. That is perspective taking and relationship skills in practice, tied to a goal everyone cares about. When a team stalls, ask the structure questions first: is the goal shared, are the roles clear, and is each member accountable?

questions.question: How would I design an AI-native day for elementary, middle, and high school?
questions.answer: The model changes by grade band. Chapter 21 describes an elementary school model, a middle school model, and a high school model, and Chapter 20 works a full middle school day. The elementary school model keeps one home-room teacher with a class for most of the day, for a stable relationship. The morning is short, mostly teacher-led and hands-on, with a brief adaptive block for reading and number practice; the afternoon is play, movement, music, stories, and projects. The middle school model adds an advisory teacher who follows a student for several years, an adaptive morning of about 150 minutes with breaks every 25 to 30 minutes, and afternoon projects with public exhibitions. The high school model builds around credits: a morning that mixes adaptive work with seminars and labs, and an afternoon of capstone projects, internships, dual enrollment, ensembles, and service, often in block scheduling of 80 to 90 minutes. Every band must still meet legal instructional-time rules and do all the jobs a school does, including meals, supervision, and support services. A design exercise is to start from a blank bell schedule and place each block against those constraints.

questions.question: Does an AI-native model pay for itself?
questions.answer: Partly, but not fully, according to the book's example. Software and content costs can fall a great deal: open Level 2 content costs very little, and the affordable Alpha model in Chapter 23 adds only about $64 per student per year after print savings for the morning. The main cost is the afternoon, which needs trained adults. Chapter 21 tests whether budget reallocation can cover it, for example by shifting spending from print textbooks and some direct-instruction time. In its example, reallocation does not fully pay for the afternoon. That means a district has to decide whether the gains in collaboration, engagement, and human skills are worth new money, or find partners such as arts organizations, community groups, and youth sports programs. A sound plan states the gap honestly rather than promising that technology savings cover everything.

questions.question: How do I plan for uncertainty in the AI forecast?
questions.answer: Chapter 5 recommends four tools. Use scenarios: write plans for a fast trend, the central trend, and a slow or stalled trend, since the doubling time drives most of the uncertainty. Prefer no-regret moves, which pay off in every scenario, such as open Level 2 content, better data governance, staff AI literacy, and a stronger afternoon program. Make decisions reversible where you can, with short contracts and data export. Set trip-wires, measurable signals that trigger a planned response, such as "if independent studies of AI tutors in our grade band show gains over two consecutive years, expand the pilot." State the prediction assumptions behind the plan and test it against a prediction failure scenario: if AI capability stalled tomorrow, what in the plan would still be worth doing? A plan that only makes sense if the trend continues is a bet, not a plan.

questions.question: How can a school keep AI costs and energy use low at scale?
questions.answer: Use AI where its cost is paid once, and avoid it where its cost is paid per student per question. Generate once, serve many pays for content creation once and serves static pages for a fraction of a cent. Adaptation without live AI uses a Learning Record Store, a mastery threshold, and a learning-graph lookup to choose each student's next step, with no model call at all. Where chat tutoring adds real value, use it selectively. In Chapter 12, limiting chatbot use to the moments a student is stuck, rather than chat for everything, cut inference cost and energy by 80 percent or more. Chapter 5 puts energy in perspective: a chatbot tutoring session uses roughly 12 watt-hours in its example, which is modest, while video generation and long agent tasks use far more. Inference cost for a fixed capability level fell more than 280-fold from November 2022 to October 2024, so selective use gets cheaper over time too.

questions.question: How would I evaluate a pilot so the result is trustworthy?
questions.answer: Build the evaluation into the pilot before it starts. Chapter 21 recommends a logic model that links resources and activities to the outcomes you expect, so you know what to measure at each stage. Choose a balanced set of success measures in advance, so no one can pick the favorable ones afterward. Use a comparison. The fairest practical design is A/B testing with delayed access: randomly choose which classes start this term, and give the program to the rest next term. That answers the ethical objection that some students are denied a benefit, since everyone gets it. Measure outcomes without AI assistance, as the Turkish study did, so that practice gains are not mistaken for learning. Check the gap between groups, not only the average. Where possible, have an independent evaluator analyze the results. Then apply the decision rule written at the start, even if the result is disappointing.

questions.question: What would a two-sided story about an AI-native school look like?
questions.answer: A two-sided story shows a benefit, a risk, and how the school responds, which is the book's risk-and-response framework in miniature. Chapter 22 reads each case as benefit, risk, response, and lesson, and Chapter 23 shows how to write one. For example: Maya, a sixth grader, moves through her math morning at her own pace and finishes a unit two weeks early (benefit). Her teacher notices that Maya has started asking the tutor for answers whenever she is stuck, and her quiz scores without the tutor are dropping (risk: cognitive offloading). The school switches the tutor to hint-first mode, adds a weekly no-AI check, and pairs Maya with a peer to explain her reasoning in the afternoon (response). The lesson is that design and adult attention, not the software alone, decide the outcome. Writing stories this way keeps a school from either hiding risks or giving up on benefits.

questions.question: How might Level 5 autonomous textbooks change schools, and what safeguards would they need?
questions.answer: A Level 5 autonomous AI textbook would generate each lesson in real time for each student, with full personalization of examples, pacing, and explanations. Chapter 6 places it as technically plausible around three years out on the central trend, but dependent on reliability and trust. The risks are new in kind. A generated lesson may contain confident errors that no editor has seen. Two students may receive different explanations of the same concept, making it harder for teachers and families to know what was taught. Full personalization needs the richest student data of any level. The book's level-specific policy for Level 5 is human review of generated lessons, on top of every safeguard from Levels 1 to 4: accessibility, simulation accuracy, governed records with bias audits, and chat guardrails. A reasonable design question is what share of generated content must be reviewed, by whom, and how fast, before a Level 5 product could be trusted with a whole course.

questions.question: How can the afternoon be equitable when families have different resources?
questions.answer: Make the afternoon part of the free school day, not an add-on families pay for. Chapter 20 lists a free afternoon among the requirements for equity of access, alongside devices, accessibility, and language support. Private models charge tuition of $40,000 to $65,000, which is the cost barrier the public model is meant to remove. Partnerships help but need care. Chapter 14 covers community partnerships with arts groups, youth sports, libraries, and local employers, with written agreements covering safety, schedules, and goals. Partnerships tend to cluster in better-resourced neighborhoods, so a district should map where they are and fill gaps deliberately. Activity-skill matching ensures every student gets a spread of skills across the week, not just the activities their friends or parents chose. Transportation, equipment, and instrument loans matter as much as the program design. El Sistema's youth orchestras, which use group music to build belonging in low-income communities, show the afternoon can serve the students with the least.
